title: Interior of the Earth and Rocks
tagline: Crust, mantle and core, and the igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks that make up the crust

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The depths, thicknesses and velocities quoted are standard values from geophysics; the simplified structure follows the three-layer model used in school geography, which is a teaching approximation of a more complicated reality. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Name the three main layers of the Earth's interior and give the depth and thickness of each.
State the evidence that led to the division of the interior into these layers.
Distinguish between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks with examples and mode of formation.
Explain the rock cycle and the economic importance of rocks and minerals.

overview.intro: Nobody has ever seen inside the Earth, and no drill has gone even a little way towards the centre, so the structure of the interior has been worked out from the behaviour of earthquake waves. The Earth is described in three layers: a thin crust, a thick mantle and a dense core. The crust is the part we live on and it is made of rock; the mantle is hot silicate rock that can flow very slowly; the core is mostly iron and nickel, with an outer part that is liquid, which is why the Earth behaves like a giant magnet. On the surface, rock takes one of three forms according to how it was formed. Igneous rock was crystallised out of molten material, sedimentary rock was laid down as layers of sediment and hardened, and metamorphic rock is older rock that has been changed by heat and pressure. These three kinds are continually being transformed into one another in the rock cycle.

facts.label: Crust
facts.value: The thin outer shell, from the surface to the Mohorovicic discontinuity at an average depth of about 32 km

facts.label: Mantle
facts.value: About 2,900 km thick, of hot silicate rock rich in silicon and magnesium

facts.label: Core
facts.value: Iron and nickel, with a liquid outer core from 2,900 km to 5,150 km and a solid inner core below that

facts.label: Discontinuities
facts.value: The Mohorovicic discontinuity separates crust from mantle and the Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle from core

learn.title: The three layers of the Earth's interior

blocks.text: The Earth is commonly taught as a three-layer structure: the crust, the mantle and the core. The crust is the outermost and thinnest layer and is the only one we can examine directly. Below it the mantle extends down to about 2,900 km and is composed of silicate rock rich in silicon and magnesium, with iron. The core lies below the mantle and is composed mainly of iron and nickel, divided into an outer core that is liquid and an inner core that is solid. The dividing surfaces are known as discontinuities: the Mohorovicic discontinuity, or Moho, separates the crust from the mantle, and the Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the core.

items.meaning: The thin rigid outer shell of the Earth, made of rock and forming the continents and the ocean floor.
The thick middle layer of the Earth, of hot silicate rock that can flow very slowly over long periods.
The liquid part of the core, from about 2,900 km to 5,150 km deep, composed of molten iron and nickel.
The innermost layer of the Earth, composed mainly of iron and nickel, with a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
A sudden change in the Earth's structure or in the speed of seismic waves, which marks a boundary between layers.

items: The continental crust is thicker and less dense than the oceanic crust, and both float on the denser mantle.
The temperature at the centre of the Earth is estimated at about 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius.
The pressure at the centre is enormous, several million times the pressure at the surface.
The mantle is solid under the weight of the overlying rock, but it deforms and creeps very slowly, which is why the tectonic plates move.
The inner core is solid rather than liquid because the immense pressure at that depth prevents the iron from melting.

learn.title: How the interior of the Earth is known

blocks.text: The evidence for the internal structure of the Earth comes almost entirely from the study of earthquake waves, together with the study of the Earth's magnetism and of the way rocks change under great pressure. Earthquake waves travel through the Earth at speeds that increase with depth, and they change speed and direction suddenly at certain depths. These sudden changes are the discontinuities. When P-waves pass through the core they slow down sharply because they enter a less rigid medium, and S-waves are stopped altogether by the liquid outer core. A shadow zone of about 104 degrees from the epicentre, in which no direct S-waves arrive, is the proof that part of the core is liquid.

items.text: Why is the Earth's core made of iron and nickel?
items.note: The best explanation is that the Earth formed from the same material as the Sun and the other planets, and the dense iron and nickel sank towards the centre during the heavy collisions and heating of the early Earth, while the lighter silicate material rose to form the mantle and crust. The presence of a solid inner core of the same composition is explained by the enormous pressure at the centre.

items: P-waves, or primary waves, are compressional and can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
S-waves, or secondary waves, are shear waves and travel only through solids, so they cannot pass through the liquid outer core.
Surface waves, the slowest and most destructive seismic waves, travel along the surface of the Earth.
The bending of seismic waves shows that the Earth is not uniform inside but is arranged in layers of different density.
The fact that the Earth behaves like a large magnet is further evidence for a metallic core.

blocks.text: Rock is classified by the process that formed it. Igneous rock was formed by the cooling and solidification of molten material, either below the ground as magma, giving intrusive or plutonic rock, or at the surface as lava, giving extrusive or volcanic rock. Sedimentary rock was formed from sediments, fragments of pre-existing rock, which were deposited in layers, compacted by the weight above and cemented by minerals dissolved in water. Metamorphic rock is any rock that has been changed in the interior of the Earth by heat and pressure, without being melted.

items: Granite is an intrusive igneous rock, formed slowly deep down, and is coarse-grained; basalt is extrusive, formed quickly at the surface, and is fine-grained.
Sedimentary rocks are the only rocks that contain fossils, so they give the best evidence of past life and of the age of rock layers.
The layers of sedimentary rock are laid down horizontally, and this is the principle used in the law of superposition.
Metamorphic rock is harder and more resistant than the rock from which it was formed, because its crystals have recrystallised.
Marble is limestone changed by heat and pressure; slate is shale changed in the same way; quartzite is sandstone changed by heat and pressure.

learn.title: The rock cycle and the importance of rocks

blocks.text: Any rock can be changed into any other rock given enough time, and this continuous recycling is called the rock cycle. Igneous rock exposed at the surface is broken down by weathering and worn away by denudation, and the fragments are carried by rivers, deposited as sediment and hardened into sedimentary rock. If that sedimentary rock is buried deeply enough, the heat and pressure of the interior turn it into metamorphic rock. If the temperature is high enough to melt it, it becomes magma again, and when that magma cools it forms igneous rock, and the cycle begins again. Any of these stages may be skipped, and the whole cycle takes millions of years.

items: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed from buried remains of plants and animals in sedimentary rock, and are called conventional sources of energy.
Metallic minerals such as iron ore, bauxite and copper ore are obtained from the Earth's crust and refined in smelters.
Non-metallic minerals such as salt, sulphur, mica and sand are used in industry, in construction and in the manufacture of glass and cement.
Building stone, clay for bricks and pottery, and limestone for cement all come from the crust.
The oldest rocks are found in the cores of the continents, and the youngest in the rift valleys and on the ocean floor.

items.text: Trace the change from granite to marble and back again.
items.note: Granite is igneous. Exposed at the surface it is broken down by weathering; the fragments are eroded, transported and deposited as sediment, which is compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock such as sandstone. If that sandstone is buried deeply and subjected to great heat and pressure, its grains are recrystallised into quartzite. Marble is the metamorphic rock formed from limestone, not from granite, so the path from granite back to marble runs granite, sediment, sandstone, quartzite, melt, magma, and then igneous rock of a new kind. This is a good illustration that the cycle has many routes.

figures.caption: Figure: Internal structure of the Earth
figures.description: The Earth is built in three layers. A thin crust of brittle rock rests on the mantle of hot silicate rock, and below the Gutenberg discontinuity lies the core of iron and nickel, with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

figures.caption: Figure: The rock cycle
figures.description: Magma cools to igneous rock, which weathers and erodes into sediments; the sediments are compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock, which is changed by heat and pressure into metamorphic rock, and melting returns it to magma.

keyPoints: The Earth's interior is divided into crust, mantle and core, with discontinuities marking the boundaries.
The crust is thin, brittle and broken into plates; it is about 35 km thick under continents and 5 to 10 km under the oceans.
The mantle extends from about 32 km to 2,900 km and is of hot silicate rock that flows very slowly.
The core is of iron and nickel; the outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid because of the enormous pressure.
S-waves travel only through solids, so their absence proves that the outer core is liquid.
Igneous rock is formed by the cooling of magma or lava; granite is intrusive and basalt is extrusive.
Sedimentary rock is formed by deposition, compaction and cementation, and is the only rock that contains fossils.
Metamorphic rock is formed by heat and pressure acting on existing rock; marble comes from limestone and slate from shale.
The rock cycle converts one type of rock into another; it may take millions of years.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels, and metallic minerals are the raw materials of industry.
examFocus: Comparison questions on the three types of rock are almost always set as a table; prepare the rows for agent of formation, layering, fossils and examples.
When asked for evidence about the interior, always mention P-waves, S-waves and the shadow zone, because the behaviour of S-waves is the strongest evidence.
Do not say the mantle is liquid. The mantle is solid but flows slowly; only the outer core is liquid.
For the rock cycle, name the process that links each pair of rocks, for example 'heat and pressure' or 'melting'.
Importance questions should separate the conventional sources of energy from metallic and non-metallic minerals, and give a use for each.

vocabulary.meaning: Molten rock below the surface of the Earth.
Molten rock that has reached the surface of the Earth.
Rock formed by the cooling and solidification of magma or lava.
Rock formed from deposited sediments that have been compacted and cemented.
Rock changed by heat and pressure without being melted.
A boundary within the Earth marked by a sudden change in seismic wave speed.
The weaker, slowly flowing part of the upper mantle on which the tectonic plates move.
The preserved remains or traces of past life, found in sedimentary rock.

questions.prompt: The boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle is called the:
questions.explanation: The Mohorovicic discontinuity, or Moho, is the surface separating the crust from the mantle. The Gutenberg discontinuity lies far below, at about 2,900 km, and separates the mantle from the core.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'Gutenberg discontinuity', which is the boundary between the mantle and the core.

questions.explanation: Fossils form in layers of sediment that bury the remains of organisms, so they are preserved in sedimentary rock. The heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock destroys them.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing metamorphic rock, because it is harder and is sometimes thought to preserve more.

questions.prompt: Granite and basalt are examples of:
questions.explanation: Both are igneous: granite is intrusive, formed by slow cooling deep in the crust, and basalt is extrusive, formed by fast cooling of lava at the surface.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing metamorphic rock, confusing the coarse-grained texture of granite with the banding of gneiss.

questions.prompt: The absence of S-waves beyond about 104 degrees from the epicentre shows that:
questions.explanation: S-waves are shear waves and travel only through solids, so they cannot pass through the liquid outer core. The shadow zone they leave behind is the main proof of that.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 'the mantle is liquid', which would stop S-waves at a much shallower depth and would not produce a shadow zone of that shape.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the rock formed by the heat and pressure acting on shale is ________.
questions.explanation: Metamorphism changes shale into slate, limestone into marble and sandstone into quartzite. Slate is used for roofing because it splits into flat sheets.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'marble', which is the metamorphic rock formed from limestone.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the molten rock that has reached the surface of the Earth is called ________.
questions.explanation: Molten rock below the surface is magma; when it reaches the surface and is ejected it is called lava. The word lava is also used for the rock that solidifies from it.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'magma', which is the molten rock below the surface.

questions.prompt: State how igneous rock is classified and give one example of each class.
questions.answer: Igneous rock is classified by where the molten rock has cooled. If it cools inside the crust it is intrusive or plutonic rock, and it cools slowly and so has large crystals; granite is an example. If it cools at the surface after being ejected it is extrusive or volcanic rock, and it cools quickly and so has small crystals and often contains gas bubbles; basalt is an example.
questions.explanation: The position of cooling decides the rate of cooling, and the rate of cooling decides the size of the crystals.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the names of the two classes without an example of each, which loses the example marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how sedimentary rock is formed.
questions.answer: The fragments of pre-existing rock, called sediments, are broken down by weathering, eroded by running water, wind or waves, and carried to a place where the flow slows down. There they are deposited in layers. The weight of the layers above compacts the lower layers, and minerals dissolved in water cement the particles together. Over a long period the loose sediment becomes hard sedimentary rock, such as sandstone, shale or limestone, and the layers are clearly bedded.
questions.explanation: The four steps to remember are deposition, compaction, cementation and lithification.
questions.commonMistake: Leaving out compaction or cementation, which are the two processes that actually turn loose sediment into rock.

questions.prompt: Explain what the rock cycle is and name the processes that link each pair of rocks in it.
questions.answer: The rock cycle is the continuous transformation of one type of rock into another over very long periods of time. Magma cools and solidifies to form igneous rock. Igneous rock exposed at the surface is broken down by weathering and removed by erosion, and the fragments are deposited as sediment, which is compacted and cemented to form sedimentary rock. Sedimentary rock that is buried deeply is changed by heat and pressure to form metamorphic rock. Metamorphic rock that is heated still further melts to form magma, and the cycle starts again. Any stage may be omitted, and the full cycle takes millions of years.
questions.explanation: The four links are cooling, weathering and deposition, heat and pressure, and melting.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that all igneous rock becomes sedimentary rock, and forgetting that metamorphic rock may melt directly back into magma.

questions.prompt: Describe the internal structure of the Earth, giving the depth and composition of each layer, and explain how seismic waves have made it possible to work it out.
questions.answer: The Earth is built in three layers. The crust is the outermost and thinnest, extending from the surface to the Mohorovicic discontinuity at an average depth of about 32 km; it is brittle rock, about 35 km thick under the continents and about 5 to 10 km under the oceans. The mantle extends from the Moho to the Gutenberg discontinuity at about 2,900 km and is of hot silicate rock rich in silicon and magnesium; it is solid but flows very slowly. The core runs from 2,900 km to the centre at 6,371 km and is of iron and nickel; its outer part, from 2,900 km to 5,150 km, is liquid and its inner part is solid because of the immense pressure. The structure was worked out from seismic waves. P-waves travel through everything but slow sharply at the core boundary because the material is less rigid. S-waves travel only through solids, and their absence in a shadow zone of about 104 degrees from the epicentre shows that the outer core is liquid. S-waves reappear beyond that zone because they pass through the solid inner core, and the bending of the waves shows that the interior is layered rather than uniform.
questions.explanation: The description and the evidence belong together: each layer is matched to the wave behaviour that reveals it.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the layers without giving the depth of each, or giving the evidence without linking it to a particular layer.

questions.prompt: Explain why sedimentary rocks give far more information about the history of the Earth than igneous or metamorphic rocks, and state one way in which this information is used.
questions.answer: Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers in a definite order, with the oldest at the bottom, because the law of superposition states that in an undisturbed sequence the lower layers are older than those above them. They are also relatively soft and are only slightly altered by heat and pressure, so they retain their original characters. Most importantly, they accumulate in the conditions in which they are formed: coarse sands and gravels mark fast-flowing water or strong wind, fine clays mark still water, and layers of salt or gypsum mark the drying up of a sea. These features are then buried and turned into rock. Igneous rocks give far less: their minerals can be dated, which tells us when they cooled, but they record nothing about the surface conditions of the time. Metamorphic rocks have been so heated and pressurised that their original structure and any fossils are largely destroyed. The information is used in relative dating, in correlating rock layers across different parts of the world, in identifying the environments in which sediments were laid down, and in locating the oil and gas reservoirs on which the world depends, because these accumulate in particular kinds of sedimentary rock.
questions.explanation: The argument rests on three properties of sedimentary rock, namely order of deposition, low alteration and the way sediments record the conditions of their formation.
questions.commonMistake: Saying only that sedimentary rock contains fossils, and not explaining that the layer itself records the conditions in which it was deposited.
